and WHEREAS, the gift establishes the Helen Izzi Schilling ’54 and Francis Schilling Scholars Program, an endowed scholarship that will provide significant financial support—up to $20,000 per year for four years—to high-achieving undergraduate students pursuing degrees in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields; and WHEREAS, this transformative scholarship program not only offers financial aid but also leadership development and mentoring, empowering students to achieve their academic and professional goals, and ensuring the future success of the University’s students in vital and innovative disciplines; and WHEREAS, Helen Izzi Schilling’s education in the sciences, which began at URI, laid the foundation for a distinguished career as a registered dietitian, educator, and businesswoman, making a significant impact on the healthcare community over five decades; and WHEREAS, Helen Izzi Schilling was deeply committed to the University and to making a difference in the lives of students, particularly those who, like her, sought careers in service to others; and WHEREAS, Francis Schilling, after completing his M.B.A. and pursuing a successful career in industry, including as vice president at GE Medical Systems, introduced pioneering medical technologies such as CT and MRI scanners to healthcare providers, demonstrating his commitment to innovation and progress; and WHEREAS, the Schilling’s extraordinary generosity is a testament to their unwavering belief in the power of education, their dedication to advancing STEM fields, and their desire to leave a legacy that will inspire future generations of students; and

WHEREAS, the Schilling’s gift further strengthens the University’s mission of providing transformative educational opportunities, adding to the momentum of URI’s recently completed comprehensive campaign, which raised over $73 million for financial aid; and WHEREAS, the Schilling family’s deep ties to Rhode Island, dating back to the early 1900s, and their ongoing commitment to the state’s future, underscore the lasting impact of their support for the University and its students; WHEREAS, the faculty will enjoy the benefits and are ready to join in force to support the development of the scores of students who will benefit from this award far into the future, WHEREAS, collaborative work with their son, Paul Schilling, with past URI President Robert Carothers, current University of Rhode Island President Marc Parlange, and the University of Rhode Island Foundation & Alumni Engagement President Lil O’Rourke fashioned this historic arrangement to benefit high achieving students in concrete and direct ways, WHEREAS, the opportunity for life-changing support for strong students from all walks of life, including those with immigration heritages such as that of Helen Izzi Schilling herself, connotes deep concern, empathy, and intergenerational support for unknown others, NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, on behalf of the entire University community, expresses its profound appreciation and heartfelt gratitude to the Schilling Family and the memories of Helen Izzi Schilling and Francis Schilling for their visionary generosity, their enduring legacy of support for URI students, and their commitment to ensuring that future generations have the tools and resources they need to achieve their highest ambitions; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this resolution be entered into the official minutes of the Faculty Senate and that a copy be sent to the Schilling family as a token of our deep appreciation.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 P ASTORE H ALL , 51 L OWER C OLLEGE R OAD , K INGSTON , R I 02881 U SA , P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-02 Faculty Senate Meeting of December 12, 2024 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS , following considerable self-study, and with significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They unite students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS , Contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences;” and WHEREAS , Honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS ,Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to a student’s interests and needs; and WHEREAS , Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED , that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously. Adopted this 12th day of December, 2024. ____________________________________________________________ Theodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

The student and instructor must agree on the criteria for evaluating the project and its scheduling. Instructors are under no obligation to supervise Honors Contracts. The Honors contract is intended to enrich the student's education by further work of mutual interest to the student and instructor, rather than simply adding to the course’s workload. Students would therefore be wise to consider projects where the enriched assignment or activity also suits the interests and needs of the instructor. Overall, plan for 3-5 hours of direct faculty involvement, including evaluation.

Honors Contracts: FAQ for Faculty For the URI Honors Program Web Page (Draft Dec. 4, 2024) What is an Honors Contract? Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. Why should we use Honors Contracts? Honors Contracts offer several beneﬁts: Flexibility: They allow students to tailor their education to their interests and goals. Accessibility: They provide opportunities for honors-level work when there are limitations on the number of honors courses offered. Student Engagement: They empower students, foster motivation, and facilitate mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. Who can supervise an Honors contract? All full-time faculty may supervise an Honors contract. No one, however, is required to do so. Part-time faculty and staff may supervise contracts only in special cases if an exception is granted prior to the creation of a contract by the Honors Program. What are the faculty roles and responsibilities in an Honors contract? Faculty roles and responsibilities include: Helping the student formulate a proposal for an appropriate contract project.

Deﬁning the terms and timeline of the contract with the student.
Providing guidance as the student works on the contracted project, with at least one mid-project meeting.
Evaluating the contract project at the end of the semester.
How much time should faculty plan to devote to this?
Generally, a faculty member should expect to devote 3-5 hours over the course of a term on a contracted project.
How are Honors Contracts set up?
The Honors Program provides comprehensive guidelines and support for setting up contracts on its Web site (See “The Contract Process”.
Students are encouraged to communicate early with instructors and the Honors Program to explore possibilities and ensure a clear understanding of the process.

What are some examples of positive outcomes from Honors Contracts?
When well-managed, Honors Contracts can: • Cultivate personalized learning experiences. • Develop strong mentoring relationships between students and faculty. • Enhance the overall honors experience. • Provide faculty with a new vision for their courses.
What are some potential problems with Honors Contracts, and how can they be avoided?
Some potential issues include: Routine or Casual Use: Contracts should not become commonplace or be considered a replacement of the regular honors curriculum.

Lack of Meaningful Interaction: Although the contracted projects require only about 20 hours of work by the student and 3 to 5 hours of work by the faculty, it is important to ensure that contracts involve meaningful interaction between students and instructors. Unclear Expectations: The Honors Program provides clear guidelines and assessment criteria to students and faculty maintain high standards. Faculty are be expected to provide clear instructions to the students in the contract language. How can I ensure that Honors Contracts are effective? To ensure effectiveness: Maintain high standards and clear expectations. Ensure that the contracted work is well-connected to the course themes and outcomes. Ensure that the contracted work enhances the student’s experience of the course themes, materials, and outcomes. Will I be compensated for my work with Honors Contracts? Yes, it is essential that faculty are recognized and compensated for the additional work involved in Honors Contracts. Your work should be noted in your review portfolio. What is the difference between an Honors contract and an Honors Project? An Honors contract deﬁnes a project requiring approximately 20 hours of work, appended to an existing non-Honors course to allow the course’s credits be counted as Honors credits. An Honors project is a mentored independent study for 3 or 6 credits, devoted to a project that requires extensive research, reading, writing, creativity, or experimentation.

How is an Honors contract satisﬁed? An Honors contract is satisﬁed when the professor notiﬁes the Honors Program that the student has completed the assigned task satisfactorily. The student must also receive a B or higher in the course in order to earn Honors credit. Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule. However, the student and instructor may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. What happens if a student fails to complete an Honors contract? If a student fails to complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor, they will not receive Honors credit for the course. Can Honors contracts be applied to all courses? No, Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor should they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses taken at other institutions.
